lessons.intro: You will learn to find the one figure in a set that does not belong. This skill trains fast visual comparison, which shows up in most shape puzzles.

cards.b: Break each shape into simple features such as the number of sides, corners and curves. Then check which feature differs across the set. Naming features keeps you accurate when the clock is running.
Quick counts of sides and corners often settle a puzzle in seconds. If two shapes match on every count, look at orientation or shading next. Counting beats guessing when shapes look alike.
Most sets follow one rule that most of the shapes obey. Find that rule using the majority, then test each shape against it. The shape that breaks the rule is your answer.

fig.title: Find the rule-breaker
fig.note: Most cells are circles. The square breaks the pattern.

ex.q: Which shape does not belong: rhombus, triangle, square, rectangle?
ex.why: Rhombus, square and rectangle each have four sides. A triangle has only three sides, so it is the odd one out.

lessons.tip: Count sides first, then corners, before comparing anything else.

quiz.q: Which is the odd one out: circle, oval, square, ring?
quiz.why: The other three shapes are curved all the way round, while the square has four straight sides.

quiz.q: Four shapes are triangles and one is a square. Which feature do the triangles share that the square lacks?
quiz.why: Each triangle has three sides, while the square has four sides and four corners.

lessons.t: Naming shapes by their number of sides
lessons.intro: You will learn how the number of sides rises as shapes grow. Spotting that pattern lets you name a shape quickly, even one you have not seen before.

cards.b: In a simple flat shape, the number of corners equals the number of sides. Checking both gives you a second way to confirm a shape. This habit catches mistakes when two shapes look similar.

Greek prefixes tell you the count: tri for three, quad for four, penta for five and hexa for six. Once you know them, you can name a shape at a glance. Prefixes work as a quick reference during a test.
When each shape adds one side, the counts rise by one each time. Recognising that step lets you predict the next figure in a series. Look for the step before you count everything.

fig.title: Sides rising one at a time
fig.note: Each shape gains one more side than the one before.

ex.q: A flat shape has 5 sides. What is its name?
ex.why: Penta means five, so a five-sided flat shape is a pentagon. A hexagon has six sides and a square has four.

lessons.tip: Say the prefix aloud, tri, quad, penta, hexa, and the count follows.

quiz.q: How many sides does a hexagon have?
quiz.why: Hexa means six, so a hexagon has six sides.

quiz.q: Which shape has the most sides?
quiz.why: A hexagon has six sides, more than the triangle (3), square (4) or pentagon (5).

lessons.intro: You will learn to find lines of symmetry, the lines that split a shape into matching halves. Symmetry is one of the fastest ways to compare two forms.

cards.h: A line splits a shape evenly
cards.b: A line of symmetry is a line you could fold along so both halves match exactly. Some shapes have one line, some have several, and some have none. Count the lines before you compare two shapes.

cards.h: Test by folding in your mind
cards.b: Imagine folding the shape along the candidate line and check whether every point lands on its partner. Capital letters like A and H have a vertical line, while a capital R has none. Test each candidate line separately.

A shape has rotational symmetry if it looks the same after a turn of less than a full circle. A square looks the same after a quarter turn of 90 degrees. Keep the two ideas apart when a puzzle mentions turning.

fig.title: Symmetric or not?
fig.note: Test each candidate line by folding it in your mind.

ex.q: How many lines of symmetry does a square have?
ex.why: A square has four lines: two through the midpoints of opposite edges and two along the diagonals. A rectangle that is not a square has only two.

lessons.tip: Fold the picture in your head before you count the lines.

quiz.q: How many lines of symmetry does an equilateral triangle have?
quiz.why: Each corner has a line running to the midpoint of the opposite side, giving three lines.

quiz.q: Which capital letter has a vertical line of symmetry?
quiz.why: A splits into two matching halves down its middle, while F, R and G do not.

lessons.t: A four-step method for testing symmetry
lessons.intro: You will learn a repeatable method for checking symmetry quickly and accurately. Following the same steps every time reduces careless mistakes in timed tests.

cards.b: Look at the outer edge first, since symmetry shows up most clearly in the outline. Note whether the top matches the bottom and the left matches the right. An uneven outline rules out most lines at once.

cards.h: Check one line at a time
cards.b: Pick one candidate line and fold the shape along it in your mind. Compare each point with its partner on the other side. Only move on once that line is confirmed or ruled out.

Write down the number of lines you have confirmed before testing the next one. Keeping a running count prevents double counting. For regular shapes, a final count that matches the number of sides is a useful check.

fig.title: Testing one shape for symmetry
fig.note: Repeat for every candidate line. Each step has a specific job.

ex.q: A regular octagon has how many lines of symmetry?
ex.why: A regular polygon has as many lines of symmetry as it has sides. An octagon has eight sides, so it has eight lines.

lessons.tip: Check the outline first, since an uneven outline rules out most lines at once.

quiz.q: A regular pentagon has how many lines of symmetry?
quiz.why: Each line runs from a corner to the midpoint of the opposite side, and there are five corners.

quiz.q: A rectangle, not a square, has how many lines of symmetry?
quiz.why: Only the two lines through the midpoints of opposite sides work, since the diagonals are not mirror lines.

lessons.intro: You will learn to test whether a shape looks the same after a turn. Rotational symmetry appears often in puzzles that ask you to match rotated figures.

cards.h: Mark a point on the shape
cards.b: Choose one corner or feature and track where it moves when you turn the shape. If the marked point lands on another matching point, the shape has rotational symmetry. Tracking one point is faster than comparing the whole outline.
Divide a full turn of 360 degrees by the smallest angle that gives a match. A square matches every 90 degrees, so it has four matching positions. This count is called its order of rotation.

cards.h: Not every turn is a match
cards.b: A rectangle only matches after a half turn of 180 degrees, not after a quarter turn. Always check the smallest angle that works before you answer. Stopping at the first match you see can give the wrong count.

fig.title: Checking rotation step by step
fig.note: Repeat the turn until the marked point returns to its start.

ex.q: A rectangle, not a square, matches after a turn of how many degrees?
ex.why: A rectangle looks the same after a half turn of 180 degrees. A quarter turn of 90 degrees gives a different shape, since its sides are unequal.

lessons.tip: Use the smallest turn that matches to find the count, not any turn that happens to match.

quiz.q: How many matching positions does an equilateral triangle have in a full turn?
quiz.why: The triangle matches every 120 degrees, and 360 divided by 120 gives three positions.

quiz.q: A regular hexagon matches after each turn of how many degrees?
quiz.why: Six equal sides and corners mean the shape matches every 60 degrees, since 360 divided by 6 is 60.

lessons.intro: You will learn to predict the next figure in a repeating sequence of shapes. These questions test whether you can detect a cycle and apply it.

cards.b: Look for the smallest group of shapes that repeats. In a row like circle, star, circle, star, the unit is two shapes long. Identify this unit before you predict anything.

cards.h: Check the position in the cycle
cards.b: Find which position the gap sits in within the unit. Use the remainder when the position number is divided by the unit length. This tells you exactly which shape comes next.
Some patterns repeat the same shape but turn it each time. Note the direction of each figure as well as its type. A changed angle can be the rule even when the shape stays the same.

fig.title: A repeating two-shape pattern
fig.note: The unit is circle then star. The gap is a circle.

ex.q: A pattern goes circle, star, circle, star, ? What comes next?
ex.why: The unit is circle then star, and it repeats. The fifth position starts a new unit, so the gap is a circle.

lessons.tip: Name the repeating unit before you guess the next shape.

quiz.q: A pattern runs A, B, C, A, B, C, A. What is the next letter?
quiz.why: The unit is three letters long, and the eighth position follows the second position of the unit, which is B.

quiz.q: A row of shapes repeats every 3 positions. Which position matches position 10?
quiz.why: 10 divided by 3 leaves a remainder of 1, so position 10 matches position 1 in the cycle.

lessons.t: Finding the one mismatch in a grid
lessons.intro: You will learn to scan a grid and find the one cell that breaks the pattern. Grid questions reward a systematic scan row by row.

cards.b: Read each row from left to right, then move to the next row. A fixed order stops you missing a cell. Doing this every time turns a messy grid into a checklist.

cards.h: Compare each cell to the majority
cards.b: Decide what most cells look like before you hunt for the odd one. Then look for the single cell that does not match that pattern. A grid usually has only one exception.
Confirm the mismatch by checking whether it breaks both its row and its column. A real exception fails both checks. This avoids picking a cell that only looks different at first glance.

fig.title: Spot the single mismatch
fig.note: Eight stars and one circle. The circle is the mismatch.

ex.q: A 3 by 3 grid holds triangles in eight cells and a square in one cell. How many triangles are there?
ex.why: The grid has nine cells in total. One cell is a square, so the other eight are triangles.

lessons.tip: Decide what most cells look like before hunting for the exception.

quiz.q: A grid has 4 rows of 4 cells. How many cells are there in total?
quiz.why: Four rows of four cells gives 4 times 4, which is 16.

quiz.q: In a grid, one cell differs from the 8 others. What is the best first step?
quiz.why: Knowing the majority pattern makes the single exception easy to spot.

lessons.intro: You will learn how the number of symmetry lines in a regular shape follows from its sides. This lets you answer symmetry questions without counting every line.

cards.h: Regular means equal sides and angles
cards.b: A regular shape has all sides the same length and all angles equal, like a square or an equilateral triangle. Irregular shapes mix lengths, which breaks symmetry. Confirm regularity before using the shortcut.

For a regular polygon, the number of lines of symmetry equals the number of sides. Each line passes through a corner and the opposite side, or through the midpoints of two opposite sides. This rule works for every regular polygon.
A rectangle is not regular, so it has only two lines of symmetry. A square is regular and has four. Always check whether the shape is regular before applying the rule.

fig.title: Lines of symmetry, regular shapes
fig.note: Each regular shape has one line per side.

ex.q: A regular heptagon has seven sides. How many lines of symmetry does it have?
ex.why: A regular polygon has one line of symmetry per side, so seven sides give seven lines. The number of corners gives the same count.

lessons.tip: For regular shapes, the line count is just the side count.

quiz.q: How many lines of symmetry does a rectangle that is not a square have?
quiz.why: A rectangle is not regular, so only the two midline folds work.

quiz.q: A regular decagon has how many lines of symmetry?
quiz.why: A decagon has ten sides, so it has ten lines of symmetry.

lessons.intro: You will learn a fast checking routine for symmetry questions with a time limit. The routine trades perfect detail for speed, then saves full checks for close calls.

cards.b: In a timed test, look at the outer edge before anything else. Most unsymmetrical shapes fail at once when the top and bottom or the left and right do not match. This takes a second and removes most options.

cards.h: Save full checks for close calls
cards.b: Only run a careful fold check when two options still look equal. Quick scans should eliminate most answers. Spending time on obvious cases wastes minutes you need later.
Once a shape clearly passes or fails a test, move on without second guessing. Changing a correct answer under pressure is a common mistake. Return to doubtful items at the end if time allows.

fig.title: A fast routine for each item
fig.note: Save the careful fold test for close calls.

ex.q: Two options both look symmetric, and you have time for one careful test. Which should you run first?
o: Count the corners of every option
Fold the closer pair in your mind
ex.why: A careful fold test settles close calls. Testing the pair that looks most alike focuses your effort where it matters.

lessons.tip: A fast scan removes most wrong answers, so save detail for close calls.

quiz.q: Which check takes the least time on a symmetry question?
o: Measuring each side with a ruler
quiz.why: The outline quickly shows whether halves can match, so it removes most unlikely answers at once.

quiz.q: After a clear answer, what is the best habit?
quiz.why: A clear answer deserves confidence, and changing it under pressure often causes errors.

lessons.t: Predicting the result of one fold
lessons.intro: You will learn how a single fold and a punch turn into a predictable pattern when you unfold the paper. This is the basis of many folding puzzles.

cards.h: The fold line is a mirror
cards.b: Marks made on a folded sheet appear copied across the fold line when you unfold it. Each mark has a partner the same distance from the fold, on the opposite side. Picture the fold as a mirror to predict positions.
One fold makes two layers, so a single punch passes through both. Each extra fold doubles the number of layers again. Count the layers before predicting the number of holes or cuts.
A fold along the middle mirrors every point across the centre line. A fold along a diagonal mirrors points in a different way. Identify the fold line first, then place each copy.

fig.title: One fold, one punch
fig.note: A single punch through two layers makes two holes.

ex.q: A sheet is folded in half once, then one hole is punched through both layers. How many holes appear when fully unfolded?
ex.why: The fold makes two layers, so one punch makes two holes. When unfolded, the two holes sit as mirror images across the fold line.

lessons.tip: Count the layers first, then mirror each mark across the fold line.

quiz.q: A sheet is folded in half twice, then one hole is punched. How many holes appear when unfolded?
quiz.why: Two folds create four layers, so one punch makes four holes.

quiz.q: A mark sits 3 cm from the fold line on one side. Where is its copy after unfolding?
quiz.why: The fold mirrors each point to the opposite side at the same distance, so the copy is 3 cm away on the other side.

lessons.intro: You will learn how two folds produce four copies of each mark. Recognising the four-part pattern lets you predict quarter folds quickly.

cards.b: Folding in half and then in half again makes four layers of paper. Anything you cut or punch passes through all four. Counting the layers gives you the number of copies immediately.
After unfolding, each quarter of the square holds one copy of the mark. The four copies are symmetric about both fold lines. Keep this symmetry in mind when placing them.
A mark at a folded corner becomes a copy at each of the four corners of the square. A mark on an edge becomes a pair across the fold. Know which feature you are copying before you predict.

fig.title: Four copies of one mark
fig.note: Each quarter holds one copy of the punched hole.

ex.q: A square is folded in half twice, then one corner is cut off. How many corners are cut when unfolded?
ex.why: Two folds give four layers, and the cut passes through all four. When unfolded, each corner of the square has one cut.

lessons.tip: Two folds give four layers, so every mark appears four times.

quiz.q: A sheet is folded into quarters, then one corner is cut. How many corners are cut when unfolded?
quiz.why: Quarter folds make four layers, so four corners are cut, one at each corner of the square.

quiz.q: How many layers does a sheet have after three folds?
quiz.why: Each fold doubles the layers: 2, then 4, then 8 after three folds.

lessons.t: Counting holes from a single punch
lessons.intro: You will learn how many holes a single punch makes when the paper has been folded several times. The count depends on the number of layers, so you can compute it directly.

cards.b: A single punch goes through every layer at the same spot. Each layer leaves its own hole, so the number of holes equals the number of layers. Count the layers first, and the hole count follows.
Each fold doubles the number of layers, starting from one. After one fold you have two layers, after two you have four, and so on. The pattern is a power of two.
When the paper unfolds, holes appear mirrored across each fold line. The holes are spread across the full sheet, not clustered in one spot. Expect copies in every section.

fig.title: Holes from one punch
fig.note: Each extra fold doubles the number of holes.

ex.q: Four folds, then one punch. How many holes are made?
ex.why: Four folds give 16 layers. One punch passes through all of them, so it makes 16 holes.

lessons.tip: Layers first, then holes: one punch always matches the layer count.

quiz.q: A sheet is folded once, then punched three times at different spots. How many holes appear in total?
quiz.why: One fold gives two layers, so each punch makes two holes, and three punches make six.

quiz.q: Five folds, then one punch. How many holes?
quiz.why: Five folds give 32 layers, since 2 to the power of 5 is 32.

lessons.t: Following the order of your folds
lessons.intro: You will learn how the order of folds changes the final shape of a sheet. Following folds in the right sequence is essential to predicting the result.

cards.b: Folding left over right and then top down can give a different shape from top down and then left over right when the edges differ. Track each fold as a separate step. Write them down if the puzzle gives a sequence.
After a fold, edges that were once inside are now on the outside. Later folds act on this new shape, not on the original sheet. Redraw the outline after every step.
To check a result, undo the last fold first and then work back to the start. Reversing the order keeps each mirror image in the right place. This is the surest way to predict unfolded positions.

fig.title: Fold, punch, then unfold
fig.note: Unfold in the reverse order of the folds.

ex.q: A strip is folded in half, then folded in half again. How many layers does it have?
ex.why: Each fold doubles the layers. The first fold makes two layers, and the second makes four.

lessons.tip: Redraw the outline after each fold, since later folds use the new shape.

quiz.q: When unfolding a sheet, which fold do you undo first?
quiz.why: Unfolding reverses the sequence, so the last fold is undone first.

quiz.q: A sheet with two folds is punched once. How many layers does the punch pass through?
quiz.why: Two folds give four layers, and one punch passes through all four.

lessons.t: Mirror images across a fold line
lessons.intro: You will learn how the direction of a fold decides where each copy lands. Vertical, horizontal and diagonal folds all mirror points, but across different lines.

cards.h: Vertical folds mirror left and right
cards.b: A fold down the middle copies every point to the opposite side at the same height. The copy sits the same distance from the fold, just on the other half. Keep the height fixed and flip only the side.

cards.h: Horizontal folds mirror up and down
cards.b: A fold across the middle copies points above to points below, keeping their horizontal position. The mirror line is horizontal, so the left and right position does not change.
A fold along a diagonal of a square swaps the horizontal and vertical positions of each point. A mark on the diagonal stays where it is. Mark the diagonal first, then reflect each point across it.

fig.title: Vertical or horizontal fold?
fig.note: Both create exact mirror images across the fold.

ex.q: A dot is placed on the left half of a sheet folded along its vertical centre. Where does its copy appear after unfolding?
o: On the right half at the same height
ex.why: The vertical fold is a mirror line, so the copy lands on the right half. It sits at the same height and the same distance from the fold.

lessons.tip: Find the mirror line first, then move each point straight across it.

quiz.q: A mark sits exactly on the diagonal fold line. Where is its copy?
quiz.why: A point on the mirror line is its own mirror image, so it stays in the same spot.

quiz.q: A dot is 2 cm to the left of a vertical fold line. How far is its copy from the fold?
quiz.why: Mirror images sit at the same distance from the fold, so the copy is also 2 cm away, on the right.

lessons.t: Tracing creases in a fold sequence
lessons.intro: You will learn to follow the crease lines left by a fold sequence. Creases show where the paper bent, and tracing them lets you rebuild the folding pattern.

cards.b: Each fold leaves a crease line where the paper bent. When you unfold, these lines remain visible and show the folding history. Read them to find which folds were made.
Each crease belongs to one fold, so match each line to the fold that made it. Two creases in the same place mean two folds used the same line. Sort the creases by their fold step.
Sketch the sheet after each fold and mark the new crease. Redrawing forces you to check each step. This makes it easy to spot a missing or extra line.

fig.title: Tracing one crease sequence
fig.note: Repeat for each fold until the sheet is fully unfolded.

ex.q: A sheet is folded in half and creased, then folded in half the other way and creased. Both folds run fully across the sheet. How many crease lines are visible when unfolded?
ex.why: Each full fold leaves one crease across the sheet. Two folds in different directions leave two crease lines, one per fold.

lessons.tip: Match every crease to the fold step that made it.

quiz.q: How many crease lines does one full fold across a sheet leave?
quiz.why: A single full fold leaves one crease where the paper bent.

quiz.q: Two folds are made along the same line. How many distinct crease lines appear?
quiz.why: Both folds run along the same line, so the paper creases in one place and leaves one visible line.

lessons.intro: You will learn to predict how many layers a sheet has after many folds. Recognising the doubling pattern lets you answer these questions without drawing each step.

cards.b: Start with one layer and double it at each fold. After n folds the number of layers is 2 to the power of n. This rule works for any sequence of simple folds.

cards.h: Build the sequence step by step
cards.b: Write down 2, 4, 8, 16 and so on, one term per fold. Listing the terms is reliable under time pressure. Stop when you reach the fold count the question asks for.
Real paper becomes too thick to fold by hand after about seven or eight folds. Puzzles assume ideal folding, so use the pure doubling rule. Answer the question as it is asked.

fig.title: Doubling layers with each fold
fig.note: Five folds give 32 layers.

ex.q: Starting with one sheet, how many layers after six folds?
ex.why: Each fold doubles the layers: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, then 64 after six folds.

lessons.tip: Doubling each step is faster than counting layers by hand.

quiz.q: How many layers does a sheet have after four folds?
quiz.why: The layers go 2, 4, 8, 16 over four folds, so the answer is 16.

quiz.q: Which fold count gives 32 layers?
quiz.why: Layers after five folds are 2 to the power of 5, which is 32.

lessons.intro: You will learn to find the missing mark in a repeating grid of crease or symbol marks. Puzzles like this combine scanning with rule finding.

cards.b: Many patterns alternate two marks along each row, so the mark flips each step. Check one full row before assuming a rule. Alternation is the simplest rule to test first.

cards.h: Test the rule down the columns
cards.b: A correct rule should work along the rows and down the columns at the same time. Check whether the pattern also alternates down each column. If it does, you can fill any missing cell with confidence.

cards.h: Read the gap from the rule
cards.b: Use the rule to predict the empty cell rather than guessing its shape. In an alternating grid, the empty cell takes the mark that matches the cell two places back. This is faster and more reliable than eyeballing.

fig.title: Alternating marks, one missing
fig.note: Marks alternate along rows and columns. Predict the gap.

ex.q: In a row that alternates x and o, the first cell is x and the second is o. What is the third cell?
ex.why: The row alternates, so after x and o the next cell returns to x. The pattern repeats every two cells.

lessons.tip: Test the rule in both the rows and the columns before you fill a gap.

quiz.q: A column alternates shaded and blank, starting shaded. What is the fourth cell?
quiz.why: Shaded, blank, shaded, blank: the fourth position is blank.

quiz.q: A grid rule works along rows but fails down columns. What should you do?
quiz.why: A valid rule must work in both directions, so you need a different rule that fits the columns too.

lessons.intro: You will learn a final checklist for confirming an unfolding answer before you commit to it. Checking the count and the positions catches most common errors.

cards.b: Work out how many layers the paper had at the moment of the punch or cut. This gives the total number of copies you should expect. A mismatch here means your answer is wrong.

Place each copy by mirroring it across the fold lines in reverse order. Check that every copy sits at the same distance from the fold as the original. Missing or doubled copies show a misplaced mirror.
Compare the number of copies you placed with the layer count from the start. The two must match exactly. A final check like this prevents most avoidable errors.

fig.title: A four-step unfolding check
fig.note: Use this list on every folding puzzle.

ex.q: A sheet with three folds is punched once. The answer lists 6 holes. Is it correct?
ex.why: Three folds give eight layers, so one punch makes eight holes. The answer of six is wrong because it misses two layers.

lessons.tip: Always check that the copy count matches the layer count.

quiz.q: A sheet with one fold is punched three times. How many holes should you expect?
quiz.why: One fold gives two layers, so each punch makes two holes, and three punches make six.

quiz.q: Which check confirms a folding answer is complete?
o: The copy count equals the layer count
quiz.why: If the copies match the layers, every layer contributed one copy, so the answer is complete.

lessons.t: Seeing an object from another side
lessons.intro: You will learn to picture an object as it would look from the front, side or top. Perspective questions ask you to match a view to a 3D object.

cards.b: The front view shows the width and height of an object, while the side view shows depth and height. Two objects with the same front can look completely different from the side. Always identify which direction a view comes from.

cards.h: Build the object in your mind
cards.b: Picture the solid object and turn it slowly to see each face. Start with the face you can see most clearly. Then add the faces that are hidden from the view you were given.
A face pointing away from the viewer cannot appear in that view. Use this rule to eliminate options that show faces the object does not have from that angle. This narrows the answer quickly.

fig.title: Front view or side view?
fig.note: Same object, two directions, two different views.

ex.q: A cube is viewed straight on from the front. How many of its faces are visible?
ex.why: From straight on, only the front face faces you. The other faces point away or sideways, so only one is visible.

lessons.tip: Ask which direction the viewer is facing before you match any view.

quiz.q: A rectangular box is viewed straight from the side. Which dimensions can you see clearly?
quiz.why: The side view shows depth and height, while the width is hidden.

quiz.q: Which view of a cube shows the most faces at once?
quiz.why: A corner view shows three faces at once, more than any straight-on or edge-on view.

lessons.intro: You will learn how many faces of a cube are visible from common viewpoints. Counting visible faces is a quick way to test a perspective answer.

cards.b: Looking directly at a cube's front face reveals only that one face. The other faces are angled away or edge on. Use this as your baseline count for a straight view.
Looking at a cube along one edge, you see two adjoining faces at an angle. This happens when the cube is turned so that a single edge faces you. Count the faces that show at a glance.
Looking at a cube from a corner, the three faces meeting at that corner are visible. Their edges form a hexagon outline. This is the largest number of faces you can see from outside the cube.

fig.title: Visible faces by viewpoint
fig.note: Faces of one cube visible from each viewpoint.

ex.q: A cube is viewed from a corner. How many faces are visible?
ex.why: A corner view shows the three faces that meet at the viewed corner. The other three faces point away from you.

lessons.tip: Corner views show three faces, which is the most from outside the cube.

quiz.q: How many faces are visible when a cube is viewed straight on?
quiz.why: Only the face pointing at the viewer is seen directly.

quiz.q: A cube is turned so one edge faces the viewer. How many faces show?
quiz.why: Viewed along an edge, two adjoining faces are visible at an angle.

lessons.t: Rotating a model in your mind
lessons.intro: You will learn to turn a 3D model around one axis in your mind. Rotation questions test whether you can keep track of faces as an object moves.

cards.b: Decide which line the object turns around before you move anything in your head. Turning around a vertical axis moves front faces to the sides. Naming the axis keeps the rotation consistent.
Mark one face in your mind and follow it through the turn. Where it lands tells you where the others go. Tracking a single face is much easier than tracking the whole model.
Most puzzles use turns of 90 degrees. Two quarter turns make a half turn, and four make a full circle. Break larger turns into quarter steps you can picture clearly.

fig.title: Turning a model step by step
fig.note: Repeat the quarter turn until the marked face returns.

ex.q: The cube turns 90 degrees to the right about a vertical axis. Where does its front face go?
ex.why: A turn about a vertical axis moves the front face sideways. Turning to the right carries it to the right side.

lessons.tip: Name the axis and turn direction before you picture the move.

quiz.q: How many quarter turns make a full circle?
quiz.why: Each quarter turn is 90 degrees, and 4 times 90 is 360.

quiz.q: A marked face starts at the front. After a half turn about a vertical axis, where is it?
quiz.why: A half turn about a vertical axis takes the front face to the back.

lessons.t: Working out hidden faces in a model
lessons.intro: You will learn to count the faces you cannot see when cubes are stacked or joined. This helps you reason about views that show only part of an object.

cards.b: In any single view, some faces of a solid are always hidden. A cube hides at least three of its six faces from any one viewpoint. Knowing how many are hidden tells you what each view can and cannot show.
When two cubes touch, their shared face disappears from the outside. Each contact removes two faces from the total visible surface. Count the contacts carefully when you check a model.
A single cube has six faces, so two separate cubes have twelve faces. Joining them removes two faces from the outside. Applying this rule gives you the exposed surface quickly.

fig.title: Counting exposed faces
fig.note: Each contact removes two faces from the exposed total.

ex.q: Two cubes touch on one face. How many faces are exposed in total?
ex.why: Two cubes have 12 faces. Touching hides one face on each cube, which leaves ten faces exposed.

lessons.tip: Each touching face pair hides two faces from the outside.

quiz.q: How many faces does a single cube have?
quiz.why: A cube has six square faces.

quiz.q: Three cubes stand in a line, each touching the next. How many faces are exposed?
quiz.why: Three cubes have 18 faces. The two contacts hide four faces in total, leaving fourteen exposed.

lessons.intro: You will learn how the apparent size of an object signals how far away it is. This principle helps you order objects by depth in a drawn scene.

cards.b: Objects of the same real size look bigger when they are closer to you. Distant objects shrink in your view. Compare sizes to judge which object sits nearer the front.
In a simplified view, doubling the distance makes an object appear half as tall. This rough rule helps you estimate how far away something sits. Use it to order a series of objects by depth.

cards.h: Overlap shows what is in front
cards.b: When one shape covers part of another, the covering shape is in front. Use overlaps together with size to decide depth. Two clues that agree give you a confident answer.

fig.title: Halving size with distance
fig.note: Each doubling of distance halves the apparent size.

ex.q: Three identical balls appear at sizes 8 cm, 4 cm and 2 cm in a series. Which is farthest?
ex.why: With real size fixed, the smallest apparent size means the greatest distance. The 2 cm ball is therefore the farthest.

lessons.tip: Smaller apparent size usually means more distance, if the real sizes match.

quiz.q: Two identical cups look 6 cm and 3 cm tall. Which is nearer?
quiz.why: The taller apparent size belongs to the closer cup, since the real size is the same.

quiz.q: An object's apparent size halves when its distance doubles. If it looks 4 cm at 10 m, what size at 20 m?
quiz.why: Doubling the distance halves the apparent size, so 4 cm becomes 2 cm.

lessons.intro: You will learn to recognise a letter or shape after it has been rotated or reflected. Many perspective puzzles hinge on telling a true turn from a mirror image.

cards.b: A rotation turns a shape without changing its handedness. A letter turned by a quarter turn still has the same left and right order. Check that the shape keeps its order before you match it.
A mirror image flips left and right, so letters like R or F look reversed. Spot reversed letters by checking where the stem or the bump sits. Reflection is the most common trick in these questions.
Pick one distinctive part, such as a tail or a notch, and locate it after the turn. Its new position tells you the rotation. Use this anchor to eliminate wrong options.

fig.title: Mirror pairs of letters
fig.note: Letters b and d are mirror images. Flip tests reveal which is which.

ex.q: Which letter is a mirror image of b when reflected left to right?
ex.why: Reflecting b left to right gives d. The stem moves from the left side to the right, and the bowl moves to the left.

lessons.tip: Reflection swaps left and right, so check the stem side for mirror images.

quiz.q: Which letter is unchanged by a left-right reflection?
quiz.why: A is symmetric from left to right, so its mirror image is the same letter.

quiz.q: Is a quarter turn of the letter F a mirror image of F?
quiz.why: A turn keeps handedness, so the turned F is not a mirror image of the original.

lessons.t: Counting cubes in a stepped stack
lessons.intro: You will learn to count cubes in a stepped stack by working layer by layer. A systematic count prevents double counts and missed cubes in perspective questions.

cards.h: Count one layer at a time
cards.b: Divide the stack into horizontal layers and count each one separately. Add the totals at the end. This keeps the count organised even when the stack looks complicated.
Some cubes sit behind others and cannot be seen from the front. Use the stated dimensions or the rows you can see to count them. A hidden cube is still part of the total.

A full rectangular block has volume equal to length times width times height. Subtract any cubes missing from the corners to get the answer. Check your count with this formula whenever it is possible.

fig.title: Cubes in each row of a stack
fig.note: A stepped stack of nine cubes in three rows.

ex.q: A stepped stack has rows of 4, 3 and 2 cubes. How many cubes are there in total?
ex.why: Add the rows: 4 plus 3 plus 2 equals 9. Counting by rows avoids missing any hidden cube.

lessons.tip: Count one layer at a time, then add the totals.

quiz.q: A block is 3 cubes long, 2 wide and 2 high. How many cubes are in the full block?
quiz.why: Volume is 3 times 2 times 2, which equals 12.

quiz.q: A full 2 by 2 by 2 block has 8 cubes. One corner cube is removed. How many remain?
quiz.why: Removing one of the eight cubes leaves seven.

lessons.intro: You will learn to picture the shape you get when a solid is sliced by a flat plane. Cross-section questions test your ability to imagine the cut without drawing it.

cards.h: A cut makes a flat face
cards.b: Slicing a solid with a flat plane produces a new flat face called a cross-section. The shape of that face depends on the angle of the cut. Picture the cut as a sheet passing through the object.
A plane cut parallel to the base of a prism gives the same shape as the base. A cube sliced parallel to a face gives a square. Use this rule to name the cross-section quickly.

A cut through a cube at an angle can give a rectangle or a triangle, depending on where it crosses the edges. Count the faces the plane crosses, since each one gives a side of the slice. Use that count to name the shape.

fig.title: Cutting a cube two ways
fig.note: The number of faces crossed sets the number of sides.

ex.q: A cube is sliced by a plane parallel to its top face. What shape is the cross-section?
ex.why: A parallel slice matches the top face, which is a square. The cut passes through four vertical edges.

lessons.tip: A slice parallel to a face copies that face's shape.

quiz.q: A plane cuts off one corner of a cube, crossing three faces. What shape results?
quiz.why: Three faces crossed give three sides, so the cross-section is a triangle.

quiz.q: A slice is made parallel to the base of a cylinder. What shape is the cross-section?
quiz.why: Cutting a cylinder parallel to its base gives a copy of the base, which is a circle.

lessons.t: Rotating around two axes at once
lessons.intro: You will learn to combine two rotations, such as a turn and a tilt, to track where a model ends up. Combined rotations are a common challenge in advanced perspective puzzles.

cards.b: When two turns are given, apply the first turn fully before the second. Changing the order can give a different final position. Write the sequence down when a puzzle lists several moves.
Mark two faces that touch along an edge, then follow both through each turn. Their final positions confirm the combined rotation. Two tracked faces are enough for most puzzles.
To verify an answer, undo the second turn and then the first. If you return to the start, your combined result is correct. This reversal check catches sign and direction errors.

fig.title: Two rotations, checked in turn
fig.note: Apply the turns in the order given, then undo them to check.

ex.q: A cube is turned 90 degrees about one axis, then 90 degrees about another. What must you do to check the final position?
o: Undo the second turn, then the first
ex.why: Undoing the moves in reverse order returns the cube to its start if your combined result is correct. Repeating a turn does not test the combined result.

lessons.tip: Undo the moves in reverse order to verify a combined rotation.

quiz.q: Does the order of two different rotations always give the same final position?
quiz.why: Rotations about different axes do not commute, so order can change the result.

quiz.q: Two turns of 90 degrees about the same axis make what total turn?
quiz.why: Two quarter turns combine into one half turn, which is 180 degrees.

lessons.t: Building a shape from three views
lessons.intro: You will learn to combine a front, side and top view into one object. This is the reverse of viewing an object, and it appears in many advanced spatial puzzles.

cards.h: Read each view for its clues
cards.b: The front view gives width and height, the side view gives depth and height, and the top view gives width and depth. Each view fixes part of the 3D shape. Write down what each one tells you before combining them.

Height appears in both the front and side views, and width appears in the front and top views. Matching these shared dimensions tells you which blocks are real. A block that conflicts with any view must be removed.
Build your candidate object and view it from each direction. Every view should match the one you were given. A mismatch in any view means the candidate is wrong.

fig.title: Combining three views
fig.note: Match each view to the object before you finalise it.

ex.q: The front view shows a shape 2 cubes wide and 1 cube tall. The side view shows 1 cube deep and 1 cube tall. Which dimension do the two views share?
ex.why: Both views show height, so the shared dimension is height. Width appears only in the front view, and depth only in the side view.

lessons.tip: Each pair of views shares one dimension, so use that overlap to check.

quiz.q: Which two dimensions does the top view show?
quiz.why: A top view looks down, so it shows the width and depth of the object.

quiz.q: A candidate object fails the side view but passes the front view. What should you do?
o: Keep it because the front matches
quiz.why: Every view must match, so a candidate that fails any view has to be rebuilt.

lessons.intro: You will bring together viewpoint, rotation and counting skills in one routine. Use this final check to review what you have learned across the perspective module.

cards.b: Decide where the viewer is standing before comparing any options. Front, side, top and corner views each show different faces. Naming the viewpoint keeps every later step grounded.

Use your counting method to verify any face or cube total, and use rotation tracking to confirm each candidate. Two independent checks agreeing give strong confidence. Do not rely on a single method when a puzzle is close.
Note which kind of error you made, such as a wrong viewpoint or a missed hidden face. Repeating this review trains you to avoid the same trap. Small regular reviews improve accuracy fastest.

fig.title: Combined perspective checklist
fig.note: Name the viewpoint, then turn and count to verify.

ex.q: A cube is viewed from a corner. The cube is then turned 90 degrees about a vertical axis, and the viewpoint stays the same. How many faces are visible?
ex.why: A turn about a vertical axis keeps the cube's corners in place as a set, so the viewer still sees a corner. A corner view shows three faces.

lessons.tip: Use two independent checks, such as counting and rotation, on close answers.

quiz.q: Which viewpoint of a cube shows exactly one face?
quiz.why: Looking straight on shows only the one face that points at the viewer.

quiz.q: What is the best way to confirm a close perspective answer?
quiz.why: Two independent methods agreeing, such as counting and rotation, give strong confidence.
